references.text: The Passover lamb in Exodus is a fundamental typology for Christ as the "Lamb of God." The lamb was to be without blemish and slaughtered to protect the people of Israel from the angel of death. John the Baptist points to Jesus as the fulfillment of this image ([ref:Exod 12:3-6|Exodus 12:3-6]).

The blood of the Passover lamb was smeared on the doorframes to spare Israel's firstborn. Jesus, as the Lamb of God, takes away the sin of the world in a similar way—through his blood ([ref:Exod 12:21-23|Exodus 12:21-23]).

Isaiah's suffering servant was "led like a lamb to the slaughter" and bore our sicknesses and sins. This is the most central Old Testament background for the expression "the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world" ([ref:Isa 53:4-7|Isaiah 53:4-7]).
The suffering servant "bore the sin of many"—a direct parallel expression to "taking away the sin of the world," which John the Baptist says about Jesus ([ref:Isa 53:12|Isaiah 53:12]).

Isaac asks Abraham, "Where is the lamb for the burnt offering?" and Abraham answers that God himself will provide a lamb. This points prophetically forward to Jesus as the lamb that God himself provides ([ref:Gen 22:7-8|Genesis 22:7-8]).

On the Day of Atonement, the high priest placed both hands on the goat and confessed the people's sins over it, so that it carried them away. The expression "takes away the sin of the world" has clear parallels to this scapegoat ritual ([ref:Lev 16:21-22|Leviticus 16:21-22]).
John the Baptist repeats his testimony: "Behold, the Lamb of God!"—a confirmation of what he said in verse 29, now directed straight at two of his disciples ([ref:John 1:36|John 1:36]).

Peter writes that believers were redeemed "with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot." This shows how the early church understood Jesus as the perfect sacrificial lamb ([ref:1 Pet 1:18-19|1 Peter 1:18-19]).
Paul writes: "For our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, Christ." This explicitly links Jesus to the Passover lamb and confirms John the Baptist's testimony ([ref:1 Cor 5:7|1 Corinthians 5:7]).

In Revelation, John sees "a Lamb standing as though it had been slain" standing right before the throne. The Lamb in Revelation is the exalted Christ, the same Lamb that John the Baptist pointed to ([ref:Rev 5:6|Revelation 5:6]).

The hymn in heaven proclaims that "the Lamb who was slain is worthy to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing." The lamb motif from John 1:29 reaches its fulfillment in this heavenly song of praise ([ref:Rev 5:12|Revelation 5:12]).

The Letter to the Hebrews explains that Christ "bore the sins of many" when he offered himself once for all. The expression "to take away sin" is directly linked to his unique sacrifice ([ref:Heb 9:26-28|Hebrews 9:26-28]).
John writes that Jesus "was revealed to take away sins," using the same Greek expression (αἴρειν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν) as in John 1:29 ([ref:1 John 3:5|1 John 3:5]).
